scenes.name: Bowie e Iggy en Berlín
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: Más que Never Mind the Bollocks o el debut de The Clash, al postpunk lo marcaron los cuatro discos de Bowie de 1977: Low y Heroes, y The Idiot y Lust for Life de Iggy Pop. Grabados en Berlín, se alejan de Estados Unidos y del rock'n'roll hacia un sonido europeo, frío y controlado, sobre los ritmos motorik de Kraftwerk y Neu!, con los sintetizadores al mismo nivel que las guitarras. El lado dos de Low, con Brian Eno («texturólogo supremo»), es una suite de atmósferas crepusculares. Eno se convierte después en uno de los productores que definen la era (no wave, Devo, Talking Heads, U2).

podcast.title: Pioneering Harmonizer Use (1977)
podcast.body: During the recording of David Bowie's *Low*, producer Tony Visconti used the iconic Harmonizer H910 multi-effects processor for the first time on the drums. He applied it to give the drums a futuristic touch, a technique that would later be widely adopted in New Wave music in the 1980s. "Besconti utilizó por primera vez el icónico procesador multi-efectos, Armonaiser H910 en la batería para darle un toque futurista, técnica que usaría la NiWave en los años 80."

srcs.source: Central Sonora

podcast.title: "Band on the Run" Orchestral Contribution
podcast.body: Paul McCartney hired Tony Visconti to both write for and conduct a 60-piece orchestra during the challenging recording sessions for the *Band on the Run* album in Nigeria. Visconti's involvement aimed to enhance the musicality despite the difficult conditions. "Paul McCartney and Tony Visconti who McCartney hired to both write for and conduct a 60 piece orchestra."

srcs.source: For the Record - The 70s
For the Record - The 70s

podcast.title: Capturing Ideas for *Heroes*
podcast.body: During the recording sessions for David Bowie's *Heroes*, which were overflowing with constantly evolving ideas often at risk of being lost, Tony Visconti kept a magnetic tape recorder running continuously to ensure no creative moment was missed. "Visconti tenía una grabadora de cinta magnética y ciencia en día durante todo el proceso para que no se perdiese nada."

podcast.title: David Bowie's *To Pimp a Butterfly* Revelation
podcast.body: Tony Visconti recounted an instance where David Bowie visited him, presenting *To Pimp a Butterfly* by Kendrick Lamar. Bowie declared, "Tony, this is what I want to do. This is the music I want to make from now on—complex music that mixes styles, breaks molds, and is written intimately." This conversation highlighted Bowie's profound inspiration from Lamar's work. "el propio Tony Visconti nos cuenta como un día el propio David Bowie va a verle con el disco y le dice Tony, esto es lo que yo quiero hacer."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Discovery of Marc Bolan
podcast.body: Tony Visconti is credited with discovering Marc Bolan, a pivotal figure in glam rock. "Prácticamente, Tony Biz Conti es la persona que descubra Mar Bolanc."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: EL PIONERO DEL GLAM: MARC BOLAN Y T REX

podcast.title: Glam Rock Production with T-Rex
podcast.body: Despite his long-standing collaboration with Bowie, Visconti did not produce Bowie's glam music albums (e.g., *Ziggy Stardust*, *Aladdin Sane*, *Pin Ups*). Instead, during that same period, Visconti was actively involved in producing albums for Marc Bolan's band T-Rex, thus playing a direct role in the birth and development of glam music. "curiosamente, Tony Biz Conti no produjo los discos de música glam que hizo David Bowie."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Marriage to May Pang
podcast.body: Tony Visconti, a producer for David Bowie, married May Pang, who was John Lennon's assistant during his "lost weekend" period from Yoko Ono. "Not only did he and Bowie get along famously but so did Lennon's assistant May Pang and Bowie producer Tony Viscante and they actually ended up getting married."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Possible Inspiration for Bowie's "Heroes"
podcast.body: Tony Visconti and his girlfriend, Antonia Maass, were possibly the young couple David Bowie saw kissing by the Berlin Wall from the studio window, an event that allegedly inspired the song "Heroes." "This was possibly producer Tony Visconti and his girlfriend, Antonio Moss."

xref.title: Secret Comeback (2011-2013)
xref.body: Bowie orchestrated his 2013 comeback album, *The Next Day*, in absolute secrecy. He worked with trusted producer Tony Visconti and a small coterie of musicians, all of whom signed non-disclosure agreements. His family and the skeleton staff at The Magic Shop studio (near his apartment) kept the secret. He had minimal staff, only his fiercely loyal personal assistant Coco Schwab and business person Bill Zysblat, with no pressure from his record label, Sony. His understanding of the internet meant he knew he could announce his return without a traditional marketing campaign, simply by dropping a hint online. "How did Bowie, one of the most famous musicians in the world that ever seen, manage that? He was working with Tony Visconti again. Tony can keep a secret."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Collaboration with Bowie on "Young Americans"
xref.body: John Lennon collaborated with David Bowie during his "last week in the Strangement" from Yoko Ono, co-writing the lyrics for the song "Fame" in about 20 minutes. He also provided background vocals, notably echoing the word "fame" in the verses of the recording for Bowie's "Young Americans" album. Lennon and Bowie got along famously, and Lennon's assistant, May Pang, later married Bowie's producer, Tony Visconti. "Not only did he and Bowie get along famously but so did Lennon's assistant May Pang and Bowie producer Tony Viscante and they actually ended up getting married."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Collaboration with John Lennon
xref.body: By 1975, Bowie was famous enough that John Lennon was willing to collaborate, co-writing the song "Fame." Lennon, in the middle of his "lost weekend" separation from Yoko Ono, happily partied and worked with Bowie. Their professional and personal relationships extended to their associates, with Lennon's assistant, May Pang, eventually marrying Bowie's producer, Tony Visconti. "By this time Bowie was big enough that someone like John Lennon was willing to hang out and even do a little co-writing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Early Band with Tony Visconti Deal
xref.body: Omaha Sheriff was Chris Berkett's band that signed a record deal with Tony Visconti for a couple of albums. "my band was called Omaha Sheriff and that was Tony became my mentor while I was in the studio."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Early Career Mentorship with Tony Visconti
xref.body: Chris Berkett signed a deal for a couple of albums with Tony Visconti and his band Omaha Sheriff. While in the studio, Berkett constantly asked Visconti questions due to his electronics degree, learning how to make records by observing him. "I learned how to make records by watching Tony."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Key Contributor to Bowie's Berlin Trilogy
xref.body: Brian Eno made significant contributions to David Bowie's albums "Low" (especially Side 2) and "Lodger" during the Berlin trilogy period. While he did not produce "Lodger" (Tony Visconti did), he played an essential role in helping Bowie explore his musical ideas. "Brian Eno was there to make some important contributions."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Visconti and Moss Inspiration for "Heroes"
xref.body: Producer Tony Visconti provided a long-standing explanation for the lyrics of "Heroes," stating that David Bowie saw him embracing German singer Antonia Moss by the Berlin Wall. Visconti, from the West, and Moss, from the East, were depicted as hating the divided city but insisting on kissing by the wall as bullets flew from guard towers. Bowie later confirmed seeing the couple. "We've been told that one of the lovers is from the west, which is Visconti, and the other from the east, which is Moss."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
